scope_plain: Every City of Pittsburgh voter. The whole city is in the 12th District, along with eastern and southern Allegheny County suburbs and part of Westmoreland County.
office_explainer: Pittsburgh's one seat in the U.S. House. Votes on federal laws, taxes and spending.
why_it_matters: A rematch of 2024, when Lee beat Hayes by nearly 13 points. Republicans hold the House 218 to 214, so each seat counts toward which party controls it.

candidates.name: Summer Lee
candidates.background: U.S. representative since 2023; before that, three terms in the state House. First Black woman to represent Pennsylvania in Congress. Law degree from Howard University; lives in Swissvale.

own_words.text: On costs: Congress must "crack down on price-gouging, stop Wall Street from buying up homes, lower prescription costs."
On immigration: "I've also called to abolish ICE and end its detention apparatus."
On data centers: growth "cannot mean handing corporations a blank check on our electricity, water, environment, or wallets."

candidates.name: James Hayes
candidates.background: Chief financial officer of Gulf Coast Sand LLC; about 30 years in finance and industry, including six years at the Federal Reserve. The Republican nominee against Lee in 2024. Lives in Shadyside.

own_words.text: On costs: "Congress should focus on the cost of producing the things American families need."
On immigration: "Enforcement should be firm, consistent and focused on public safety rather than political theater."
On data centers: Congress should "encourage American innovation while making sure growth does not overwhelm our electrical grid."

scope_plain: City of Pittsburgh voters in Wards 10, 11 and 12 (East End neighborhoods including Highland Park, Morningside, Garfield, East Liberty and Lincoln-Lemington-Belmar), plus North Hills and Allegheny River suburbs. Only even-numbered Senate seats are up this year; city voters in the 43rd District (Wards 4, 5, 7, 8, 13 to 18 and 29 to 31) have no state Senate race.
office_explainer: One of 50 state senators. Writes Pennsylvania laws and votes on the state budget.
why_it_matters: Williams, the top Democrat on the Senate Education Committee, is seeking a third four-year term. Republicans have controlled the state Senate for more than 30 years.

candidates.name: Lindsey Williams
candidates.background: State senator since winning the seat in 2018; minority chair of the Senate Education Committee and a Pittsburgh Regional Transit board member. Lawyer and former political director for the Pittsburgh Federation of Teachers. Lives in West View.

own_words.text: Biggest local concern: "how unaffordable everything is right now."
On data centers: her bill SB 724 "would require developers to invest no less than 10% of the total project cost back into the community."
On new state revenue: "I'm the prime sponsor of the digital advertisement tax in the Senate."

candidates.name: Thomas West
candidates.background: Has owned TRIM Pittsburgh, a men's clothing store in Lawrenceville, for about 12 years; former TV news producer. Ran in the 2025 Republican primary for Pittsburgh mayor. Lives in Highland Park.

own_words.text: Biggest local concern: property taxes and reassessment. "I support statewide standards for regular, predictable reassessments."
On data centers: "I support a temporary pause on new hyperscale data centers while Pennsylvania establishes clear rules."
On new state revenue: backs legal adult-use marijuana and taxing skill games, but "I do not support a new digital-advertising tax."

scope_plain: A small part of the City of Pittsburgh (parts of Wards 26 and 27: Brighton Heights, Perry North and some of Summer Hill), plus Ross Township, Avalon, Bellevue and West View.
office_explainer: One of 203 state representatives. Writes Pennsylvania laws and votes on the state budget.
why_it_matters: Kinkead has held the seat since 2021. Aguglia got on the ballot through a write-in campaign in the May primary. Democrats hold the state House 103 to 100, so every seat counts toward control.

candidates.name: Emily Kinkead
candidates.background: First elected to the state House in 2020. Lawyer and former Commonwealth Court law clerk; chairs Allegheny County's sewer authority. Lives in Brighton Heights.

own_words.text: Biggest local concern: landslides. She wants to expand state mine-subsidence insurance "to include landslides or create a free-standing insurance program."
On new revenue from cannabis, digital ads and skill games: "I support all of them."
On private-school tax credits: "Public money for public schools unless private schools submit to the same transparency and regulation."

candidates.name: Joseph Aguglia
candidates.background: Senior legal compliance officer at a transportation brokerage; former assistant district attorney and former director of the Erie County Human Relations Commission. Won the Republican nomination by write-in in May. Lives in Ross Township.

own_words.text: Biggest local concern: "I would propose property tax reform and relief as being the #1 local issue not addressed by Harrisburg."
On new revenue: tax skill games at 20% and use "100% of this tax ... in place of property taxes."
On private-school tax credits: "I am not in favor of cutting funding for EITC, or putting up excessive barriers to funding."

why_it_matters: Benham has held the seat since 2021 and ran unopposed in the spring primary. Democrats hold the state House 103 to 100, so every seat counts toward control.

candidates.name: Jessica Benham
candidates.background: State representative since 2021; former development director of the Pittsburgh Center for Autistic Advocacy. Ph.D. from the University of Pittsburgh. Lives in the South Side Slopes.

own_words.text: Top focus: "continue to make it easier for people to afford to live a good life in the Commonwealth."
On new revenue: "I do support the taxation of recreational cannabis."
On private-school tax credits: "Public money, public schools."

candidates.name: Timothy McCune
candidates.background: Pediatric home health aide and a volunteer firefighter from 2005 to 2023; founded the nonprofit Safety Net of Hope. First-time candidate. Lives in Brentwood.

own_words.text: Biggest local concern: aging roads, stormwater and volunteer emergency services; wants more "state grants for municipal infrastructure and Fire/EMS operations."
On new revenue: favors legal cannabis, skill games and digital-ad taxes, but the money "must directly offset state-imposed fees."
On private-school tax credits: supports "targeted educational choice for students with IEPs."

scope_plain: A small part of the City of Pittsburgh (Ward 31: Hays, Lincoln Place and New Homestead), plus Baldwin, Whitehall, Dravosburg, Glassport and part of West Mifflin.
office_explainer: One of 203 state representatives. Writes Pennsylvania laws and votes on the state budget.
why_it_matters: A rematch of 2024, when Inglis won the open seat by 11 points. Democrats hold the state House 103 to 100, so every seat counts toward control.

candidates.name: John Inglis
candidates.background: First elected to the state House in 2024; former teacher and school counselor in the West Mifflin Area School District and West Mifflin borough councilman (2018 to 2024). Lives in West Mifflin.

own_words.text: Biggest local concern: "The biggest issue facing most of my constituents, Pennsylvanians, and Americans is affordability."
On new revenue: "I am a prime sponsor of the digital advertising tax aimed at making mega corporations pay their fair share."
On private-school tax credits: "I am opposed to school vouchers."

candidates.name: Stone Sobieralski
candidates.background: Stonemason; served one term on Whitehall borough council and on its planning commission. Lost to Inglis in 2024 and won this year's Republican nomination by write-in. Lives in Whitehall. Campaign is on Facebook and Instagram (stoneforpa); no website found.

own_words.text: Biggest local concern: "Our most pressing local concern is fair school funding."
On new revenue: "I do not and will never support creating new taxes simply to give Harrisburg more money to spend."
On private-school tax credits: "I am a strong supporter of school choice."
